statement: Every finite [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $s$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) is $s=\mu-\nu$ for [finite measures](c:finite-measure) $\mu,\nu$ that are [mutually singular](c:singular-measure), and this pair is unique.

hypotheses.text: The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a [measurable space](c:measurable-space).
The map $s\colon\mathcal A\to\mathbb R$ is a [signed measure](c:signed-measure): it is countably additive and $s(\emptyset)=0$.

conclusion: There are mutually singular finite measures $\mu,\nu$ on $\mathcal A$ with $s=\mu-\nu$, and $s$ determines them.

formal.difference: The declaration states $s=\text{posPart}-\text{negPart}$ for the pair that `toJordanDecomposition` builds from a Hahn decomposition. Mutual singularity sits in the `JordanDecomposition` structure, and uniqueness is the separate declaration `JordanDecomposition.toSignedMeasure_injective`.

proofs.name: Split along a Hahn decomposition
proofs.slogan: Split the space into a positive and a negative set, and let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be $s$ and $-s$ restricted to them.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a real-valued signed measure: steps 1 to 4 prove existence and step 5 proves uniqueness.

roles.why: The sets $P$, $N$ and all $A\cap P$ are measurable sets of the given space.
Countable additivity makes $\mu$ and $\nu$ measures and lets $s(A)$ split along $P$ and $N$.

steps.slogan: Split the space by a Hahn decomposition for $s$.
steps.detail: The [Hahn decomposition](c:is-hahn-decomposition) theorem gives a measurable set $P$ such that $s(B)\ge0$ for every measurable $B\subseteq P$ and $s(B)\le0$ for every measurable $B\subseteq N=X\setminus P$.

steps.slogan: Define the positive and negative parts by restricting $s$ to $P$ and $N$.
steps.detail: Put $\mu(A)=s(A\cap P)$ and $\nu(A)=-s(A\cap N)$. Both are nonnegative by step 1 and vanish on $\emptyset$. They are countably additive because $s$ is, so they are [finite measures](c:finite-measure).

steps.slogan: Check that $\mu$ is zero on $N$ and $\nu$ is zero on $P$.
steps.detail: We have $\mu(N)=s(N\cap P)=s(\emptyset)=0$ and $\nu(P)=-s(P\cap N)=0$. So $\mu$ and $\nu$ are concentrated on the disjoint sets $P$ and $N$, which means they are [mutually singular](c:singular-measure).

steps.slogan: Split each measurable set along $P$ and $N$ and add the two values.
steps.detail: For measurable $A$, additivity gives $s(A)=s(A\cap P)+s(A\cap N)$, since $A\cap P$ and $A\cap N$ are disjoint with union $A$. This equals $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$, so $s=\mu-\nu$.

steps.slogan: Show that any other mutually singular decomposition gives the same pair.

Let $s=\mu'-
u'$ with $\mu'$ and $
u'$ concentrated on disjoint sets $P'$ and $N'$. Then $(P',N')$ is also a Hahn decomposition, so on $P	riangle P'$ the value of $s$ is both $\ge0$ and $\le0$, hence $0$. Therefore $\mu'(A)=s(A\cap P')=s(A\cap P)=\mu(A)$, and $

concepts.c:finite-measure: Restricting a real-valued $s$ to $P$ or $N$ gives finite positive measures.
concepts.c:is-hahn-decomposition: The Hahn decomposition fixes the positive set $P$ and the negative set $N$.
concepts.c:measurable-space: It supplies the sets on which $s$, $\mu$ and $\nu$ are defined.
concepts.c:signed-measure: The theorem splits this set function into two positive parts.
concepts.c:singular-measure: The two parts live on the disjoint sets $P$ and $N$.

statement: Over a field $k$, every [A-infinity algebra](c:a-infinity-algebra) $A$ (for example a dg algebra) is A-infinity [quasi-isomorphic](c:quasi-isomorphism) to its cohomology $H(A)$ carrying a transferred structure with $m_1=0$ and $m_2$ the induced product.

hypotheses.text: The ground ring $k$ is a field.
The object $A$ is an [A-infinity algebra](c:a-infinity-algebra) over $k$, for example a [differential graded algebra](c:differential-graded-algebra).

conclusion: The [cohomology](c:cohomology) $H(A)$ has a [minimal](c:minimal-model) A-infinity structure with $m_1=0$ and $m_2$ the induced product, and an A-infinity quasi-isomorphism $H(A)\to A$ whose first component picks cocycle representatives.

proofs.name: Obstruction induction on the arity
proofs.slogan: Build the operations $m_n$ on $H(A)$ and the morphism components $f_n$ arity by arity, killing each obstruction cocycle with a contraction.
proofs.scope: An outline of Kadeishvili's published proof; the sign computation that the obstruction is a cocycle (step 3) rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: Over a field, cocycles and coboundaries have complements, so a contraction of $A$ onto $H(A)$ exists.
The A-infinity relations of $A$ make each obstruction $\Theta_n$ a cocycle.

steps.slogan: Choose a contraction of $A$ onto its cohomology.
steps.detail: Over a field, pick cocycle representatives $i\colon H(A)\to A$, a projection $p\colon A\to H(A)$ and a degree $-1$ map $h$ with $\mathrm{id}-ip=dh+hd$. Then $pi=\mathrm{id}$, and $i$ induces the identity on [cohomology](c:cohomology).

steps.slogan: Look for $m_n$ and $f_n$ one arity at a time, starting from $f_1=i$.
steps.detail: Set $m_1=0$ and $f_1=i$. For $n\ge2$ the arity-$n$ equation of an A-infinity morphism reads $d f_n=\Theta_n-i\,m_n$, where $\Theta_n$ collects the terms built from $m^A_r$, the $f_k$ and the $m_k$ with $k<n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the obstruction $\Theta_n$ is a cocycle of $A$.
steps.detail: The A-infinity relations of $A$, together with the relations for the $m_k$ and the morphism equations in arities below $n$, give $d\Theta_n=0$. This is a direct computation with signs, done in the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Set $m_n=p\,\Theta_n$ and $f_n=h\,\Theta_n$.
steps.detail: Because $d\Theta_n=0$, the contraction identity gives $\Theta_n=ip\Theta_n+dh\Theta_n$, which is exactly $df_n=\Theta_n-i\,m_n$. The A-infinity relation for $m_n$ holds because its image under $i$ is a cocycle and a boundary, so it is zero in $H(A)$.

steps.slogan: Check that $f$ is an A-infinity quasi-isomorphism onto the structure on $H(A)$.
steps.detail: All $m_n$ and $f_n$ are defined, so $(H(A),m)$ is an A-infinity algebra with $m_1=0$, and $m_2$ is the product induced by $m_2^A$. The first component $f_1=i$ induces the identity on cohomology, so $f$ is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) and $H(A)$ is a [minimal model](c:minimal-model) of $A$.

concepts.c:a-infinity-algebra: The theorem transfers an A-infinity structure and builds an A-infinity morphism.
concepts.c:cohomology: The cohomology $H(A)$ carries the transferred structure.
concepts.c:differential-graded-algebra: A dg algebra is the basic example of an A-infinity algebra.
concepts.c:minimal-model: A structure with $m_1=0$ on $H(A)$ is a minimal model of $A$.
concepts.c:quasi-isomorphism: The built morphism has first component inducing the identity on cohomology.

source.ref: T. V. Kadeishvili, On the homology theory of fibre spaces, Uspekhi Mat. Nauk 35 (1980), no. 3, 183-188; Russian Mathematical Surveys 35 (1980), no. 3, 231-238
source.note: The same transfer is given by tree formulas in Kontsevich and Soibelman, and in Loday and Vallette, Algebraic Operads, Section 9.4 (homotopy transfer theorem). An English text is on arXiv as math/0504437.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) of complex dimension $n$ with [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) $K_X$, and $L$ a [positive line bundle](c:positive-line-bundle) on $X$. Then $H^q(X,K_X\otimes L)=0$ for every $q>0$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) of complex dimension $n$.
The holomorphic line bundle $L$ is [positive](c:positive-line-bundle): it has a Hermitian metric $h$ whose curvature form $i\Theta_h$ is a positive $(1,1)$-form.

conclusion: The [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) groups $H^q(X,K_X\otimes L)$ vanish for all $q>0$.

proofs.name: Hodge theory and the Nakano identity
proofs.slogan: Represent each class by a harmonic $L$-valued $(n,q)$-form, and show with the Nakano identity that positive curvature forces it to be zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The Kähler hypothesis is automatic, since $i\Theta_h$ is itself a Kähler form, and compactness makes the integrations by parts valid.

roles.why: Compactness gives the Hodge theorem and the integrations by parts, and the Kähler condition gives the Nakano identity.
The positive curvature supplies the metric $\omega$ and the sign of the commutator term.

steps.slogan: Take the curvature form of $L$ as the Kähler metric.
steps.detail: Choose $h$ with $\omega=i\Theta_h>0$. The form $\omega$ is closed, because a Chern curvature form is closed, so it is a Kähler form on $X$. Use $\omega$ and $h$ for all adjoints and Laplacians below.

steps.slogan: Represent each class by a harmonic form with values in $L$.
steps.detail: By Dolbeault's theorem, $H^q(X,K_X\otimes L)\cong H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial}(X,L)$, the [Dolbeault cohomology](c:dolbeault-cohomology) of $L$-valued $(n,q)$-forms. The Hodge theorem gives a $\Delta_{\bar\partial}$-[harmonic](c:harmonic-form) representative of every class, so it suffices to show that such forms vanish.

steps.slogan: Compare the two Laplacians by the Nakano identity.
steps.detail: On $L$-valued forms, $\Delta_{\bar\partial}-\Delta_{\partial_h}=[i\Theta_h,\Lambda]$, where $\Lambda$ is the adjoint of wedging with $\omega$. For $\omega=i\Theta_h$ the commutator $[\omega\wedge,\Lambda]$ is multiplication by $p+q-n$ on $(p,q)$-forms.

steps.slogan: Show that a harmonic $(n,q)$-form with $q>0$ has norm zero.
steps.detail: If $\Delta_{\bar\partial}\alpha=0$, then $0\le\langle\Delta_{\partial_h}\alpha,\alpha\rangle=-\langle[i\Theta_h,\Lambda]\alpha,\alpha\rangle=-q\,\|\alpha\|^2$, using $p=n$. Since $q>0$, this forces $\|\alpha\|=0$, so the form $\alpha$ is zero.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every cohomology class is zero.
steps.detail: Each class in $H^q(X,K_X\otimes L)$ has a harmonic representative, and that representative is zero by step 4. So the group vanishes for every $q>0$.

concepts.c:canonical-bundle: The twist $K_X\otimes L$ turns the cohomology into $(n,q)$-forms with values in $L$.
concepts.c:dolbeault-cohomology: Dolbeault's theorem identifies the sheaf cohomology with $\bar\partial$-cohomology of $L$-valued forms.
concepts.c:harmonic-form: Each class has a harmonic representative, and the proof shows that it is zero.
concepts.c:kahler-manifold: Positivity makes $i\Theta_h$ a Kähler form, which the Nakano identity needs.
concepts.c:positive-line-bundle: Positive curvature gives the sign that forces harmonic forms to vanish.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The groups to be shown zero are sheaf cohomology groups.

source.note: Kodaira's argument as in Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry (1978), Chapter 1, Section 2 (Kodaira vanishing); Kodaira, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 39 (1953), 1268-1273.

statement: Let $F\to E\xrightarrow{p}B$ be a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) and $R$ a commutative ring. Suppose each $H^n(F;R)$ is a finitely generated [free module](c:free-module) and classes $c_j\in H^{*}(E;R)$ restrict to a basis of $H^*(F;R)$ on every fibre. Then $H^*(E;R)$ is a free module over $H^*(B;R)$ with basis $\{c_j\}$.

hypotheses.text: The map $p\colon E\to B$ is a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) with fibre $F$.
Each $H^n(F;R)$ is a finitely generated [free module](c:free-module) over the commutative ring $R$.
The classes $c_j\in H^{k_j}(E;R)$ restrict to a basis of $H^*(F;R)$ on each fibre $F$.

conclusion: The map $\Phi\colon H^*(B;R)\otimes_R H^*(F;R)\to H^*(E;R)$ with $b\otimes i^*c_j\mapsto p^*b\cup c_j$ is an isomorphism, so the $c_j$ are a basis over the [cohomology ring](c:cohomology-ring) of $B$.

proofs.name: Induction over the cells of the base
proofs.slogan: Compare $\Phi$ with the Künneth map over each cell, then pass to finite and infinite [CW complexes](c:cw-complex) by the five lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The case of a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) base is proved first, and a general base is reduced to it by CW approximation.

roles.why: The bundle is trivial over each cell, and it is a Serre fibration, so pullbacks of connected maps stay connected.
Freeness of $H^*(F)$ keeps the long exact sequences exact after tensoring and gives the Künneth formula.
The classes $c_j$ define $\Phi$ and make it the Künneth map on a trivial bundle.

steps.slogan: Define $\Phi$ for every subspace of the base and for pairs.
steps.detail: For $A\subseteq B$ and $E_A=p^{-1}(A)$, set $\Phi_A(\sum b_{j}\otimes i^*c_j)=\sum p^*b_j\cup c_j|_{E_A}$. This is well defined because the $i^*c_j$ form a basis, and the same formula works for pairs $(B,A)$ and commutes with restrictions and connecting maps.

steps.slogan: Check that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism over one cell.
steps.detail: Over $(D^k,\partial D^k)$ the bundle is $D^k\times F$ and the classes $c_j$ restrict to a basis on the fibre. Since $H^*(F)$ is free, the Künneth formula for $(D^k,\partial D^k)\times F$ shows that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Induct over the cells to treat a finite-dimensional CW base.
steps.detail: For the pair $(B^k,B^{k-1})$ both sides have long exact sequences, exact on the left side because $H^*(F)$ is free, and $\Phi$ maps one to the other. If $\Phi$ is an isomorphism for $B^{k-1}$ and for the cells, the five lemma gives it for $B^k$.

steps.slogan: Pass to infinite-dimensional CW bases through the skeleta.
steps.detail: The inclusion $B^{k+1}\to B$ is $(k+1)$-connected. So $E_{B^{k+1}}\to E$ is $(k+1)$-connected by the homotopy exact sequences, and both inclusions induce isomorphisms on $H^j$ for $j\le k$. Hence $\Phi_B$ equals $\Phi_{B^{k+1}}$ in degrees $\le k$, and it is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Reduce an arbitrary base to a CW complex by approximation.
steps.detail: Take a CW approximation $B'\to B$ and pull the bundle back to $E'\to B'$. The map $E'\to E$ is a weak homotopy equivalence by the homotopy exact sequences, so it is an isomorphism on cohomology, and $\Phi_B$ is identified with $\Phi_{B'}$.

concepts.c:cohomology-ring: The base cohomology ring acts on $H^*(E)$ through $p^*$ and the cup product.
concepts.c:cw-complex: Induction runs over cells, and a general base is replaced by a CW complex.
concepts.c:fibre-bundle: Local triviality over cells and the homotopy sequence reduce the theorem to cells.
concepts.c:free-module: Freeness makes tensoring with $H^*(F)$ exact and allows the Künneth formula.

source.note: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 4D.1 (Leray-Hirsch) and its proof; originally Leray and Hirsch, late 1940s.

statement: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [solvable Lie algebra](c:solvable-lie-algebra) over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) of characteristic $0$, and $\pi\colon\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ a representation on a finite-dimensional space $V$. Then $V$ has a flag of $\pi(\mathfrak g)$-invariant subspaces with all quotients of dimension $1$; so $V$ has a basis in which every $\pi(x)$ is upper triangular.

hypotheses.text: The [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ is [solvable](c:solvable-lie-algebra).
The field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) of characteristic $0$.
The map $\pi\colon\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is a representation on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$.

conclusion: There is a [flag](c:flag) $V=V_0\supset V_1\supset\dots\supset V_n=0$ with $\dim V_i=n-i$ and $\pi(x)V_i\subseteq V_i$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the common eigenvector (a nontrivial weight space for some functional), and it replaces algebraic closure by the triangularizable hypothesis. The flag follows by induction on $\dim V$ and is not part of this declaration.

proofs.name: Induction through a codimension one ideal
proofs.slogan: Find a common eigenvector by induction on $\dim\mathfrak g$ through a codimension one ideal, then repeat on the quotient to get the flag.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $V\ne0$ (for $V=0$ the flag is trivial). Step 1 makes $\mathfrak g$ finite dimensional, and steps 2 to 4 give a common eigenvector.

roles.why: Solvability gives $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\ne\mathfrak g$ and passes to the image and to ideals.
Characteristic $0$ lets us divide by $\dim U$, and algebraic closure gives an eigenvector of $\pi(z)$.
The image of $\pi$ is finite dimensional, and the representation passes to invariant subspaces and quotients.

steps.slogan: Replace $\mathfrak g$ by its image in $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$.
steps.detail: The image $\pi(\mathfrak g)$ is a quotient of $\mathfrak g$, so it is solvable, and it is finite dimensional because $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is. So assume $\dim\mathfrak g<\infty$ and prove by induction on $\dim\mathfrak g$ that $V\ne0$ has a common eigenvector; for $\dim\mathfrak g=0$ any nonzero vector works.

steps.slogan: Find an ideal $A$ of codimension $1$ and a weight space of $A$.
steps.detail: Since $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\ne\mathfrak g$, choose a hyperplane $A\supseteq[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$; it is an ideal and solvable. By induction there is $\chi_0\colon A\to k$ whose [weight space](c:weight-space) $W=\{v:av=\chi_0(a)v\ \forall a\in A\}$ is nonzero.

steps.slogan: Show that the weight space $W$ is stable under all of $\mathfrak g$.
steps.detail: Let $w\in W$, $a\in A$, $z\in\mathfrak g$, and $U=\operatorname{span}\{w,zw,z^2w,\dots\}$. On $U$, every $a'\in A$ has $a'-\chi_0(a')$ nilpotent, and $[a,z]\in A$, so $\operatorname{tr}_U[a,z]=\chi_0([a,z])\dim U$, while a commutator has trace $0$. In characteristic $0$ this gives $\chi_0([a,z])=0$, hence $a(zw)=\chi_0(a)zw$.

steps.slogan: Find a common [eigenvector](c:eigenvector) for $\mathfrak g$ inside $W$.
steps.detail: Write $\mathfrak g=A\oplus kz$. The operator $\pi(z)$ acts on $W\ne0$, and over an algebraically closed field it has an eigenvector $v\in W$. This $v$ is an eigenvector of every $a\in A$ and of $z$, hence of all of $\mathfrak g$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the quotient by the eigenvector line and repeat.
steps.detail: The line $kv$ is invariant, so $\mathfrak g$ acts on $V/kv$, which has smaller dimension. By induction on $\dim V$ the quotient has an invariant flag; its preimages together with $0\subset kv$ form such a flag of $V$, and an adapted basis makes every $\pi(x)$ upper triangular.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: It gives an eigenvector for the extra operator $\pi(z)$.
concepts.c:eigenvector: The common eigenvector spans the first invariant line of the flag.
concepts.c:flag: The flag of invariant subspaces is what the theorem constructs.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The induction runs over the dimension of the Lie algebra and its ideals.
concepts.c:solvable-lie-algebra: Solvability gives an ideal of codimension $1$ that is again solvable.
concepts.c:weight-space: The common eigenvectors of the ideal form a weight space that is $\mathfrak g$-stable.

source.note: Follows mathlib: reduce to the image toEnd k L V, induct on dim L through a coatom ideal containing the derived algebra (exists_forall_lie_eq_smul_of_isSolvable_of_finite), show that the weight space is stable by the trace argument (weightSpaceOfIsLieTower, exists_nontrivial_weightSpace_of_lieIdeal), then take an eigenvector of z. The flag step is not in mathlib's declaration.

statement: Let $\mathcal L$ be a regular abstract logic that extends [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic). If $\mathcal L$ is countably compact and has the downward Löwenheim-Skolem property, then every $\mathcal L$-sentence is equivalent to a first-order sentence.

hypotheses.text: The logic $\mathcal L$ extends [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic), is closed under negation, conjunction, relativization and renaming of symbols, and is invariant under isomorphism.
The logic $\mathcal L$ is countably compact: a countable set of sentences, all of whose finite subsets have models, has a model.
The logic $\mathcal L$ has the downward Löwenheim-Skolem property: every satisfiable sentence has a countable model.

conclusion: Every $\mathcal L$-sentence is equivalent to a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) sentence, so $\mathcal L$ is no stronger than first-order logic.

proofs.name: Countable partially isomorphic models
proofs.slogan: If a sentence were not first-order, compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem would give two countable structures that disagree on it yet are partially isomorphic, hence isomorphic.
proofs.scope: An outline of Lindström's published proof by contradiction; the coding of the partial isomorphisms (step 3) and the passage to countable models (step 4) rest on the cited work.

roles.why: Relativization and the Boolean connectives express the sentence on two parts, and isomorphism invariance gives the contradiction.
Compactness turns the satisfiable finite stages into one structure with all stages at once.
Löwenheim-Skolem makes the two structures countable.

steps.slogan: Assume a sentence $\varphi$ with no first-order equivalent over a finite vocabulary.
steps.detail: A sentence mentions only finitely many symbols, so suppose $\varphi\in\mathcal L(\tau)$ with $\tau$ finite. We derive a contradiction from the assumption that no [first-order sentence](c:first-order-sentence) is equivalent to $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Find models on both sides of $\varphi$ that agree up to quantifier rank $n$.
steps.detail: For finite $\tau$ there are finitely many first-order sentences of rank $\le n$ up to equivalence, and each class of $n$-equivalent structures is defined by one of them. If $\varphi$ never separated two $n$-equivalent structures, it would be a finite disjunction of such sentences. So there are $A_n\models\varphi$ and $B_n\not\models\varphi$ with $A_n\equiv_nB_n$.

steps.slogan: Code each pair in one sentence that includes a system of partial isomorphisms.
steps.detail: Take two copies of $\tau$, unary symbols $P,Q$ and relation symbols $I_0,I_1,\dots$. The sentence $\psi_n$ says that $\varphi$ holds on $P$, fails on $Q$, and that $I_0,\dots,I_n$ form a back-and-forth system of partial isomorphisms. Relativization and the Boolean connectives express this, and the Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé theorem makes $\psi_n$ satisfiable.

steps.slogan: Combine compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem to get countable partially isomorphic structures.
steps.detail: Every finite set of the sentences $\psi_n$ has a model, so compactness gives one structure with $\varphi$ true on $P$, false on $Q$ and a full back-and-forth system between them. The cited proof then uses the downward Löwenheim-Skolem property to pass to countable $A\models\varphi$ and $B\not\models\varphi$ that keep this system.

steps.slogan: Make the countable structures isomorphic and contradict the choice of $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Two countable structures joined by a back-and-forth system are isomorphic, by building the isomorphism along enumerations of both. By isomorphism invariance of $\mathcal L$, $A\models\varphi$ forces $B\models\varphi$, a contradiction. So $\varphi$ is equivalent to a first-order sentence.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: It is the logic that every sentence of $\mathcal L$ is shown to reduce to.
concepts.c:first-order-sentence: Finitely many first-order sentences of bounded rank describe each class of structures.

source.ref: P. Lindström, On extensions of elementary logic, Theoria 35 (1969), 1-11
source.note: A textbook proof is in H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum and W. Thomas, Mathematical Logic (Springer, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics), Chapter XII on Lindström's theorem.

statement: Let $X$ be a [Polish space](c:polish-space), $Y$ a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) and $f\colon X\to Y$ a continuous injective map. Then the image $f(X)$ is a [Borel set](c:borel-set) of $Y$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [Polish](c:polish-space): separable and completely metrizable.
The space $Y$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
The map $f\colon X\to Y$ is continuous and injective.

conclusion: The set $f(X)$ is a [Borel subset](c:borel-set) of $Y$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any measurable structure on the target in which open sets are measurable, which is the Borel statement. It does not include the stronger form for Borel maps on Borel subsets.

proofs.name: Borel separation of the images of basic sets
proofs.slogan: Separate the images of disjoint basic open sets by Borel sets, and show that the image is a countable intersection of Borel sets built from them.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; $X=\emptyset$ is trivial, so take $X\ne\emptyset$ with a countable basis of nonempty open sets $s_i$ and a complete metric.

roles.why: A countable basis gives countably many sets $s_i$, and completeness turns a Cauchy sequence into a limit point.
Two distinct points $f(z)$ and $x$ have disjoint open neighborhoods $V$ and $W$.
Injectivity makes images of disjoint sets disjoint, and continuity makes them analytic and keeps $f(s_i)$ inside $V$.

steps.slogan: Separate the images of disjoint basic open sets by Borel sets.
steps.detail: For disjoint $s_i,s_j$, the sets $f(s_i)$ and $f(s_j)$ are disjoint, since $f$ is injective, and [analytic](c:analytic-set), since $f$ is continuous. The Lusin separation theorem gives a Borel set $q_{ij}$ with $f(s_i)\subseteq q_{ij}$ and $q_{ij}\cap f(s_j)=\emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Build Borel sets $E_i$ and $F_n$ from closures and the separating sets.
steps.detail: Let $E_i=\overline{f(s_i)}\cap\bigcap_{s_j\cap s_i=\emptyset}(q_{ij}\setminus q_{ji})$, a countable intersection of Borel sets. For $u_n\downarrow0$, let $F_n=\bigcup\{E_i:\operatorname{diam}s_i\le u_n\}$, a countable union, so $\bigcap_nF_n$ is Borel.

steps.slogan: Show that the image lies in every $F_n$.
steps.detail: Given $y\in X$ and $n$, pick a basic set $s_i\ni y$ of diameter at most $u_n$. For each $s_j$ disjoint from $s_i$, $f(y)\in q_{ij}$ and $f(y)\notin q_{ji}$, so $f(y)\in E_i\subseteq F_n$.

steps.slogan: Turn a point of every $F_n$ into a Cauchy sequence in $X$.
steps.detail: If $x\in\bigcap_nF_n$, then $x\in E_{i_n}$ with $\operatorname{diam}s_{i_n}\le u_n$. The sets $s_{i_m}$ and $s_{i_n}$ meet, since disjoint ones would put $x$ in $q_{ij}\setminus q_{ji}$ and in $q_{ji}\setminus q_{ij}$. So points $y_n\in s_{i_n}$ satisfy $d(y_m,y_n)\le u_m+u_n$ and form a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) with a limit $z$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f(z)=x$ by separating $f(z)$ from $x$.
steps.detail:
If $f(z)
e x$, take disjoint open $V
i f(z)$ and $W
i x$. By continuity $f(s_{i_n})\subseteq V$ for large $n$, so $x\in\overline{f(s_{i_n})}\subseteq\overline V$, which misses $W$, a contradiction. So $x=f(z)\in f(X)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the image equals the Borel set $\bigcap_nF_n$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 to 5 give $f(X)\subseteq\bigcap_nF_n\subseteq f(X)$, so $f(X)=\bigcap_nF_n$. By step 2 this is a [Borel set](c:borel-set).

concepts.c:analytic-set: Images of open sets are analytic, so the separation theorem applies.
concepts.c:borel-set: The image is written with countable unions, intersections and closures of Borel sets.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Points chosen in shrinking overlapping pieces form a Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: It separates the points $f(z)$ and $x$ by disjoint open sets.
concepts.c:polish-space: Completeness and a countable basis give the Cauchy argument and countable unions.

source.note: Follows mathlib, which follows Fremlin, Measure Theory vol. 4, 423I: AnalyticSet.measurablySeparable gives the sets q, then the sets E and F, a Cauchy sequence by cauchySeq_of_le_tendsto_0', and t2_separation for the contradiction.

statement: Let $E$ be a real [vector space](c:vector-space), $s\subseteq E$ a [convex cone](c:convex-cone) and $p\subseteq E$ a subspace with $p+s=E$. If a linear $f\colon p\to\mathbb R$ is nonnegative on $p\cap s$, then $f$ extends to a linear $g\colon E\to\mathbb R$ that is nonnegative on $s$.

hypotheses.text: The set $s$ is a [convex cone](c:convex-cone) in the real vector space $E$: it is closed under addition and under multiplication by nonnegative scalars.
The subspace $p$ satisfies $p+s=E$.
The linear map $f\colon p\to\mathbb R$ is nonnegative on $p\cap s$.

conclusion: There is a linear map $g\colon E\to\mathbb R$ with $g|_p=f$ and $g(x)\ge0$ for all $x\in s$, a [positive linear functional](c:positive-linear-functional) on the cone.

formal.difference: The declaration takes $s$ to be a pointed cone (a convex cone containing $0$) and writes $p+s=E$ as: for every $y$ some $x\in p$ has $x+y\in s$. Since $p$ is a subspace this is the same condition.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma and one-dimensional extension
proofs.slogan: Extend $f$ by one vector at a time, choosing the new value between two bounds, and let Zorn's lemma finish the extension.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Steps 3 and 4 assume that the maximal domain $D$ differs from $E$, and step 5 shows that this is impossible.

roles.why: Sums of elements of $s$ compare the two bounds, and positive scalars rescale the test vectors.
It makes both bound sets nonempty, so a value between them exists.
It puts $f$ in the poset and starts every chain, and it orders the two bounds.

steps.slogan: Order the extensions of $f$ that stay nonnegative on the cone.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of linear maps $g\colon D\to\mathbb R$, with $D\supseteq p$ a subspace, that extend $f$ and satisfy $g\ge0$ on $D\cap s$. Order $\mathcal P$ by extension. It contains $f$, so it is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Take a maximal element of $\mathcal P$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: The union of a chain is a linear map on the union of the domains, which is a subspace, and it is nonnegative on $s$ because each point lies in one member's domain. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal $(D,g)$. We show that $D=E$.

steps.slogan: Pick a new vector $y\notin D$ and a value $c$ between two bounds.
steps.detail: Let $S_+=\{g(x):x\in D,\ x+y\in s\}$ and $S_-=\{g(x):x\in D,\ -x-y\in s\}$. Both are nonempty because $D+s=E$. If $x_++y\in s$ and $-x_--y\in s$, then $x_+-x_-\in D\cap s$, so $g(x_-)\le g(x_+)$, and hence some $c$ has $\sup S_-\le c\le\inf S_+$.

steps.slogan: Extend by $g'(x+ty)=g(x)-tc$ and check nonnegativity on the cone.
steps.detail: Let $x+ty\in s$ with $x\in D$. For $t=0$ use $g\ge0$ on $D\cap s$; for $t>0$ we have $x/t+y\in s$, so $g(x/t)\ge c$; for $t<0$ we have $-x/|t|-y\in s$, so $g(-x/|t|)\le c$. Scaling gives $g(x)-tc\ge0$ in the last two cases.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the maximal domain is the whole space.
steps.detail: The map $g'$ lies in $\mathcal P$ and strictly extends $g$ whenever $D\ne E$, which contradicts maximality. So $D=E$, and $g$ is a linear map on $E$ extending $f$ and nonnegative on $s$.

concepts.c:convex-cone: Sums and positive scalars let the two bounds be compared and rescaled.
concepts.c:positive-linear-functional: The extension $g$ is positive on the cone $s$.
concepts.c:vector-space: The extension is built one dimension at a time in a real vector space.

source.note: Follows mathlib: RieszExtension.step extends by one vector with a value between sSup and sInf of two image sets, and RieszExtension.exists_top applies Zorn's lemma (zorn_le_nonempty₀) to partial linear maps.

statement: Let $g,h\in\mathbb C[x]$ with [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure) $M(h)\ge1$, and $f=gh$. Then for every $n\ge0$ the coefficient $g_n$ of $x^n$ in $g$ satisfies $|g_n|\le\binom{\deg g}{n}M(f)$, with a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient).

hypotheses.text: The polynomials $g,h\in\mathbb C[x]$ have product $f=gh$.
The factor $h$ has [Mahler measure](c:mahler-measure) $M(h)\ge1$, as every nonzero integer polynomial does.

proofs.name: Vieta's formulas and the roots outside the unit disc
proofs.slogan: Write each coefficient of $g$ as an elementary symmetric sum of its roots, bound each term by the Mahler measure, and then compare $M(g)$ with $M(gh)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $g=0$ or $n>\deg g$, then $g_n=0$ and the bound holds, so take $g\ne0$ and $0\le n\le d=\deg g$.

roles.why: The factorization lets $M(g)$ be compared with $M(f)$.
The condition $M(h)\ge1$ turns $M(g)M(h)$ into a bound by $M(g)$ from above.

steps.slogan: Factor $g$ over its [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) and write its Mahler measure.
steps.detail: Write $g=a\prod_{i=1}^d(x-\alpha_i)$ over $\mathbb C$, with leading coefficient $a$. By definition, $M(g)=|a|\prod_i\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$.

steps.slogan: Write the coefficient $g_n$ as an elementary symmetric sum of the roots.
steps.detail: Vieta's formulas give $g_n=(-1)^{d-n}a\,e_{d-n}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d)$. The sum $e_{d-n}$ has $\binom{d}{d-n}=\binom dn$ terms, each a product of $d-n$ distinct roots.

steps.slogan: Bound each product of roots by the product of all $\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$.
steps.detail: A product of $d-n$ roots has modulus at most the product of $\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$ over those roots. Enlarging the index set to all roots multiplies by further factors that are at least $1$.

steps.slogan: Add the bounds to get $|g_n|\le\binom dn M(g)$.
steps.detail: The triangle inequality over the $\binom dn$ terms gives $|g_n|\le|a|\binom dn\prod_i\max(1,|\alpha_i|)=\binom dn M(g)$.

steps.slogan: Pass from $M(g)$ to $M(gh)$ by multiplicativity.
steps.detail: The roots of $gh$ are those of $g$ and $h$, so $M(gh)=M(g)M(h)$. Since $M(h)\ge1$ and $M(g)\ge0$, $M(g)\le M(gh)$. Hence $|g_n|\le\binom dn M(gh)$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: It counts the products of roots in the elementary symmetric sum.
concepts.c:mahler-measure: It equals $|a|\prod\max(1,|\alpha_i|)$, which bounds every coefficient, and it is multiplicative.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The coefficients of $g$ are symmetric functions of its roots.

source.note: Follows mathlib: norm_coeff_le_choose_mul_mahlerMeasure bounds the coefficient through coeff_eq_esymm_roots_of_card and a powersetCard sum, then mahlerMeasure_mul and le_mul_of_one_le_right compare M(g) with M(gh).

statement: Let $\mathcal U$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) of a [paracompact space](c:paracompact-space) $X$ whose nonempty finite intersections are all [contractible](c:contractible-space), a [good open cover](c:good-open-cover). Then $X$ is [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to the [Čech nerve](c:cech-nerve) $N(\mathcal U)$, a [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [paracompact](c:paracompact-space), so each open cover has a subordinate partition of unity.
The family $\mathcal U$ is a [good open cover](c:good-open-cover): every nonempty finite intersection of its members is [contractible](c:contractible-space).

conclusion: The space $X$ is [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence) to the nerve $N(\mathcal U)$.

proofs.name: A glued space over both $X$ and the nerve
proofs.slogan: Build a space that maps to $X$ and to the nerve, and show that both projections are homotopy equivalences.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Paracompactness is used only for the projection to $X$, and contractibility only for the projection to the nerve.

roles.why: It gives the locally finite partition of unity that makes $s$ continuous.
Contractible intersections make each piece over a simplex homotopy equivalent to a point.

steps.slogan: Glue the pieces $U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma$ over the simplices of the nerve.
steps.detail: For each simplex $\sigma=\{i_0,\dots,i_k\}$ of $N(\mathcal U)$, let $U_\sigma=U_{i_0}\cap\dots\cap U_{i_k}$. Let $\Delta X_{\mathcal U}$ be the union of the pieces $U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma$, glued along faces. Its two projections are $p\colon\Delta X_{\mathcal U}\to X$ and $q\colon\Delta X_{\mathcal U}\to N(\mathcal U)$.

steps.slogan: Build a section $s$ of $p$ from a partition of unity.
steps.detail: Choose a locally finite [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) $(\varphi_i)$ subordinate to $\mathcal U$. Send $x$ to the point over the simplex $\{i:\varphi_i(x)>0\}$ with barycentric coordinates $(\varphi_i(x))$. This gives a continuous $s\colon X\to\Delta X_{\mathcal U}$ with $ps=\mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ is a homotopy equivalence with inverse $s$.
steps.detail: The fibre of $p$ over $x$ is the simplex on $\{i:x\in U_i\}$. The straight-line homotopy $(x,t)\mapsto(x,(1-\tau)t+\tau\varphi(x))$ stays inside these simplices and deforms the identity of $\Delta X_{\mathcal U}$ to $sp$. So $p$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Show that $q$ is a homotopy equivalence by gluing contractible pieces.
steps.detail: Over each simplex, $q$ is the projection $U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma\to\Delta^\sigma$ with $U_\sigma$ [contractible](c:contractible-space), a homotopy equivalence. A gluing lemma for homotopy equivalences along cofibrations, applied skeleton by skeleton and then to the union, makes $q$ a homotopy equivalence.

steps.slogan: Compose the two equivalences to compare $X$ with the nerve.
steps.detail: The map $s$ is a homotopy inverse of $p$, and $q$ is a homotopy equivalence. So $q\circ s\colon X\to N(\mathcal U)$ is a homotopy equivalence.

concepts.c:cech-nerve: The nerve records which members of the cover meet.
concepts.c:contractible-space: Contractible pieces make each map $U_\sigma\times\Delta^\sigma\to\Delta^\sigma$ a homotopy equivalence.
concepts.c:good-open-cover: It makes every piece over a simplex of the nerve contractible.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The theorem gives one, and the proof composes two of them.
concepts.c:open-cover: The nerve and the glued space are built from the members of this cover.
concepts.c:paracompact-space: It gives a locally finite partition of unity for the section $s$.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: It gives the barycentric coordinates of the section $s$.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The nerve is a simplicial complex whose simplices carry the pieces.

source.note: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Section 4.G (Corollary 4G.3, the nerve theorem for a paracompact space); the construction goes back to Borsuk (1948), Weil (1952) and Segal (1968).

statement: Let $L$ be a smooth Lagrangian of finite order for fields $\varphi^i$ on an open set of $\mathbb R^d$, with [Euler-Lagrange](c:euler-lagrange-equation) expressions $E_i$. Suppose the action is invariant under the [gauge symmetry](c:gauge-symmetry) $\delta_\varepsilon\varphi^i=\sum_\alpha R^{i\alpha}_a\partial_\alpha\varepsilon^a$ for every compactly supported $\varepsilon$. Then $\sum_{i,\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial_\alpha(R^{i\alpha}_aE_i)=0$ identically.

hypotheses.text: The action $S[\varphi]=\int L\,dx$ has finite-order smooth Lagrangian $L$, and $E_i=\delta S/\delta\varphi^i$ are its [Euler-Lagrange](c:euler-lagrange-equation) expressions.

For every field $\varphi$ and every compactly supported $\varepsilon^a$, the first variation of $S$ along the [gauge](c:gauge-symmetry) variation $\delta_\varepsilon\varphi^i=\sum_\alpha R^{i\alpha}_a\partial_\alpha\varepsilon^a$ is zero.

conclusion: For each $a$, $\sum_{i,\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial_\alpha(R^{i\alpha}_aE_i)=0$ holds identically, without using the field equations.

proofs.name: First variation and integration by parts
proofs.slogan: Write the first variation of the action along the gauge variation, move all derivatives off $\varepsilon$, and use that $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary.
proofs.scope: A local statement on an open set of $\mathbb R^d$ for a finite-order Lagrangian and gauge operator, valid off shell. Compact support of $\varepsilon$ removes all boundary terms.

roles.why: It gives the first variation formula $\delta S=\int E_i\,\delta\varphi^i\,dx$.
Invariance makes the first variation vanish for every compactly supported $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Write the first variation of the action as $\int E_i\,\delta\varphi^i\,dx$.
steps.detail: For a compactly supported variation $\delta\varphi$, differentiate $S[\varphi+t\,\delta\varphi]$ at $t=0$ and integrate by parts. The compact support leaves no boundary term, so $\delta S=\int E_i\,\delta\varphi^i\,dx$ with $E_i$ the [Euler-Lagrange](c:euler-lagrange-equation) expression.

steps.slogan: Insert the gauge variation and use the invariance of the action.
steps.detail: The variation $\delta_\varepsilon\varphi^i=\sum_\alpha R^{i\alpha}_a\partial_\alpha\varepsilon^a$ has compact support. Invariance under the [gauge symmetry](c:gauge-symmetry) says $\delta S=0$, so $\int E_i\sum_\alpha R^{i\alpha}_a\,\partial_\alpha\varepsilon^a\,dx=0$ for all compactly supported $\varepsilon^a$.

steps.slogan: Move every derivative from $\varepsilon$ onto the product $R\,E$ by integration by parts.
steps.detail: Because $\varepsilon$ has compact support, $\int R^{i\alpha}_aE_i\,\partial_\alpha\varepsilon^a\,dx=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int\partial_\alpha(R^{i\alpha}_aE_i)\,\varepsilon^a\,dx$. Hence $\int P_a\,\varepsilon^a\,dx=0$ for all $\varepsilon$, where $P_a=\sum_{i,\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial_\alpha(R^{i\alpha}_aE_i)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $P_a$ vanishes because $\varepsilon^a$ is arbitrary.
steps.detail: Fix $\varphi$ and suppose $P_a(x_0)>0$. Then $P_a>0$ on a ball, and a nonnegative bump function $\varepsilon^a$ supported there gives $\int P_a\varepsilon^a\,dx>0$, a contradiction; the case $<0$ is the same. So $P_a[\varphi]\equiv0$ for every $\varphi$, and since the jet of $\varphi$ at a point is arbitrary, $P_a=0$ as a differential function.

concepts.c:euler-lagrange-equation: The Euler-Lagrange expressions $E_i$ appear in the first variation and in the identity.
concepts.c:gauge-symmetry: The invariance under arbitrary $\varepsilon(x)$ is what produces a relation among the $E_i$.

source.note: The standard derivation of the second Noether theorem: E. Noether, Invariante Variationsprobleme, Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen (1918), 235-257; see also Olver, Applications of Lie Groups to Differential Equations, Chapter 5.

statement: Let $M$ be a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) and $n\ge1$. The Pontryagin construction is a bijection from the [cohomotopy](c:cohomotopy) set $[M,S^n]$ of homotopy classes of maps onto the set of [framed](c:framed-manifold) [cobordism](c:cobordism) classes of framed submanifolds of codimension $n$ in $M$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold): compact, smooth and without boundary.
The integer $n\ge1$ and $S^n$ is the $n$-[sphere](c:sphere).

conclusion: Sending a smooth map $f$ to $f^{-1}(y)$ for a [regular value](c:regular-value) $y$, framed by $df$, is a well-defined bijection onto framed cobordism classes.

proofs.name: Preimage of a regular value and the Thom collapse
proofs.slogan: Take preimages of regular values to get framed submanifolds, and collapse the complement of a tubular neighborhood to get the inverse.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for smooth maps; continuous maps are homotopic to smooth ones, so $[M,S^n]$ can be computed with smooth maps and smooth homotopies.

roles.why: Compactness gives a compact preimage and a tubular neighborhood, and it lets Sard's theorem apply on $M$ and $M\times[0,1]$.
The target $S^n$ fixes the codimension $n$ and gives the collapse map to $\mathbb R^n\cup\{\infty\}$.

steps.slogan: Pull back a regular value to get a framed submanifold.
steps.detail: By Sard's theorem a smooth $f\colon M\to S^n$ has a [regular value](c:regular-value) $y$. Then $N=f^{-1}(y)$ is a closed submanifold of codimension $n$, and $df$ identifies its normal bundle with $N\times T_yS^n$, which gives a framing.

steps.slogan: Show that the framed cobordism class ignores $y$ and the homotopy class of $f$.
steps.detail: Take a smooth homotopy $F\colon M\times[0,1]\to S^n$ between $f_0,f_1$. By Sard's theorem choose $y$ regular for $F$, $F_0$ and $F_1$; then $F^{-1}(y)$ is a framed cobordism between the two preimages. Two regular values of one $f$ are joined by a rotation of $S^n$, which changes $f$ by a homotopy.

steps.slogan: Build the inverse by collapsing the complement of a tubular neighborhood.
steps.detail: A framed $N\subset M$ has an embedding $N\times\mathbb R^n\to M$ onto a [tubular neighborhood](c:tubular-neighborhood), by the tubular neighborhood theorem and the framing. Send $(x,v)$ with $|v|<1$ to the corresponding point of $\mathbb R^n\subset S^n=\mathbb R^n\cup\{\infty\}$, and the rest of $M$ to $\infty$. The map $f_N$ has regular value $0$ with $f_N^{-1}(0)=N$ and the given framing.

steps.slogan: Turn a framed cobordism into a homotopy of collapse maps.
steps.detail: If $W\subset M\times[0,1]$ is a framed cobordism from $N_0$ to $N_1$, its collapse map is a homotopy from $f_{N_0}$ to $f_{N_1}$. A map $f$ with regular value $y$ is homotopic to $f_{f^{-1}(y)}$, by shrinking the neighborhood on which $f$ agrees with the framing.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the construction is a bijection between the two sets.
steps.detail: Step 2 makes the map $\Phi$ from $[M,S^n]$ to framed cobordism classes well defined. Step 3 gives $\Phi[f_N]=[N]$, so $\Phi$ is onto. By step 4, $[f]=[f_{f^{-1}(y)}]$ depends only on the class of $f^{-1}(y)$, so $\Phi$ is injective.

concepts.c:closed-manifold: Compactness makes the preimage compact and gives the tubular neighborhood a uniform size.
concepts.c:cobordism: Framed cobordism is the equivalence relation that matches homotopy of maps.
concepts.c:cohomotopy: The set $[M,S^n]$ of homotopy classes of maps is the cohomotopy set.
concepts.c:framed-manifold: A framing of the normal bundle is the extra data that records the map.
concepts.c:regular-value: A regular value makes the preimage a submanifold with a framing.
concepts.c:sphere: The target $S^n$ has a point $\infty$ and charts $\mathbb R^n$ for the collapse map.
concepts.c:tubular-neighborhood: A framed submanifold has a neighborhood $N\times\mathbb R^n$ to collapse onto the sphere.

source.note: L. S. Pontryagin, 1938 and 1955; Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint (1965), Section 7, Framed cobordism; the Pontryagin construction.

statement: Let $M$ be a connected smooth manifold and $D\subseteq TM$ a smooth subbundle that is [bracket-generating](c:bracket-generating-distribution): iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) of sections of $D$ span $T_qM$ at every $q$. Then any two points of $M$ are joined by a piecewise smooth path whose velocity lies in $D$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is connected.
The set $D\subseteq TM$ is a smooth subbundle, called a distribution.

The distribution $D$ is [bracket-generating](c:bracket-generating-distribution): the values at $q$ of iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) of sections of $D$ span $T_qM$ for every $q\in M$.

conclusion: For all $p,q\in M$ there is a piecewise smooth path from $q$ to $p$ with velocity in $D$ (a horizontal path).

proofs.name: Orbits of horizontal flows are open
proofs.slogan: Apply the orbit theorem to the horizontal vector fields: bracket generation makes every orbit open, and connectedness leaves one orbit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $\operatorname{rank}D$ constant and $\dim M\ge1$; paths are concatenations of finitely many flow segments of sections of $D$, which are smooth and horizontal.

roles.why: A connected manifold cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open orbits.
Flows of sections of $D$ have velocity in $D$, so their concatenations are horizontal paths.
It gives $\mathrm{Lie}_p=T_pM$, so each orbit has full dimension.

steps.slogan: Take all smooth sections of $D$ and the points reached by their flows.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal F$ be the smooth sections of $D$; then $X\in\mathcal F$ implies $-X\in\mathcal F$. The orbit $\mathcal O_q$ is the set of points $e^{t_kX_k}\cdots e^{t_1X_1}(q)$ with $X_i\in\mathcal F$, $t_i\in\mathbb R$. Each such point is joined to $q$ by a piecewise smooth horizontal path.

steps.slogan: Apply the orbit theorem to the family $\mathcal F$.
steps.detail: The Nagano-Sussmann theorem says that $\mathcal O_q$ is an immersed submanifold of $M$ whose tangent space at $p$ contains $\mathrm{Lie}_p(\mathcal F)$, the span of the values at $p$ of all iterated [Lie brackets](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) of fields in $\mathcal F$.

steps.slogan: Show that every orbit has full dimension and is open.
steps.detail: If $D$ is [bracket-generating](c:bracket-generating-distribution), then $\mathrm{Lie}_p(\mathcal F)=T_pM$ at every $p$. So $\dim\mathcal O_q=\dim M$, and an immersed submanifold of full dimension is an open subset.

steps.slogan: Split $M$ into disjoint open orbits.
steps.detail: Orbits are the classes of an equivalence relation, which is symmetric because $-X\in\mathcal F$. So $M$ is a disjoint union of open orbits, and each orbit is also closed, since its complement is a union of other open orbits.

steps.slogan: Use connectedness to show that a single orbit fills $M$.
steps.detail: A connected space is not a disjoint union of two or more nonempty open sets. So $M$ is a single orbit, and every $p\in M$ is joined to $q$ by a piecewise smooth horizontal path by step 1.

concepts.c:bracket-generating-distribution: It makes every orbit have full dimension, hence be open.
concepts.c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields: Brackets of horizontal fields add the missing directions to the orbit tangent space.

source.note: P. K. Rashevsky (1938) and W.-L. Chow (1939) proved the theorem; the orbit-theorem route is in Agrachev, Barilari and Boscain, A Comprehensive Introduction to Sub-Riemannian Geometry (Cambridge University Press, 2020).

statement: Let $a_1\le\dots\le a_n$ and $b_1\le\dots\le b_n$ be real numbers and $\sigma$ a [permutation](c:permutation) of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Then $\sum_i a_ib_{n+1-i}\le\sum_i a_ib_{\sigma(i)}\le\sum_i a_ib_i$.

hypotheses.text: The reals $a_1\le\dots\le a_n$ form a [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence).
The reals $b_1\le\dots\le b_n$ form a monotone sequence in the same order.
The map $\sigma$ is a [permutation](c:permutation) of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.

conclusion: The sum $\sum_i a_ib_{\sigma(i)}$ is largest for $\sigma=\mathrm{id}$ and smallest for $\sigma(i)=n+1-i$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves the upper bound only, for functions that monovary on a finset with values in an ordered module, which is more general than two sorted lists. The lower bound is the separate antivary version.

proofs.name: Induction by exchanging two terms
proofs.slogan: Fix the largest index by exchanging two values of $\sigma$, which cannot lower the sum, and reduce to $n-1$.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$ and every permutation, with the upper bound proved by induction on $n$ and the lower bound derived from it; for $n\le1$ there is only one sum.

roles.why: Its order gives $a_j\le a_n$ in every exchange.
Its order gives $b_{\sigma(n)}\le b_n$ in every exchange and makes the reversed list $-b_{n+1-i}$ sorted.
The permutation is changed by one exchange at a time until it fixes $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that pairing larger with larger gives the larger two-term sum.
steps.detail: For $x\le x'$ and $y\le y'$, the difference $(xy+x'y')-(xy'+x'y)$ equals $(x'-x)(y'-y)$, which is nonnegative since both factors are. So $xy'+x'y\le xy+x'y'$.

steps.slogan: Induct on $n$ and look at the largest index.
steps.detail: Assume the upper bound for $n-1$ and let $\sigma$ be a [permutation](c:permutation) of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. If $\sigma(n)=n$, then $\sigma$ restricts to $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$, and the induction hypothesis together with the equal last term gives the bound.

steps.slogan: Exchange two values of $\sigma$ so that the result fixes $n$.
steps.detail: If $\sigma(n)\ne n$, let $j=\sigma^{-1}(n)<n$ and let $\tau$ equal $\sigma$ except $\tau(j)=\sigma(n)$ and $\tau(n)=n$. Step 1 with $x=a_j\le x'=a_n$ and $y=b_{\sigma(n)}\le y'=b_n$ gives $\sum_ia_ib_{\sigma(i)}\le\sum_ia_ib_{\tau(i)}$.

steps.slogan: Chain the exchange with the case of a fixed last index.
steps.detail: The permutation $\tau$ fixes $n$, so the case $\sigma(n)=n$ gives $\sum_ia_ib_{\tau(i)}\le\sum_ia_ib_i$. With step 3 this proves $\sum_ia_ib_{\sigma(i)}\le\sum_ia_ib_i$ for every $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Reverse the second list to get the lower bound.
steps.detail: The list $b'_i=-b_{n+1-i}$ is also nondecreasing. Apply the upper bound to $a,b'$ and the permutation $i\mapsto n+1-\sigma(i)$: it reads $-\sum_ia_ib_{\sigma(i)}\le-\sum_ia_ib_{n+1-i}$, which is the lower bound.

concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Sorted order of both lists makes every two-term exchange nonnegative.
concepts.c:permutation: The sum is compared over all rearrangements $\sigma$ of the second list.

source.note: Follows mathlib: induction_on_max_value picks the index with the largest value, composes sigma with swap a (sigma a), and smul_add_smul_le_smul_add_smul' is the two-term inequality.
